kf: Drug reactions are common: first **classify the morphology** (maculopapular, urticarial, blistering, pustular, fixed, photosensitive, lichenoid).
Build a **drug timeline**: everything started in the last 8 weeks, including OTC and herbal products.
Latency clues: urticaria/anaphylaxis minutes–hours; AGEP hours–2 days; MDE 4–14 days; SJS/TEN 4–28 days; DRESS 2–8 weeks.
Red flags: **mucosal involvement, skin pain, blisters, facial oedema, fever, organ dysfunction**: same-day referral.
Stop the likely culprit, document the reaction precisely, Yellow Card serious reactions, and refer for allergy testing when it matters.
myths: **"Any rash on amoxicillin = penicillin allergy"**: many are viral or non-allergic; mislabelled allergy harms future care.
patho_lead: Drug reactions follow **different immune pathways**, which explain their timing and appearance.

mech.t: Mast cell degranulation within minutes: urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis.
Delayed days to weeks: maculopapular (IVb/c), SJS/TEN (IVc), AGEP (IVd), DRESS (IVb).
mech.cap: Delayed drug reaction: a drug held by an antigen-presenting cell activates a T cell, whose cytokines damage keratinocytes.

mech.t: Some drugs bind HLA or T-cell receptors directly; HLA alleles predict risk (HLA-B*58:01, B*15:02, B*57:01).
Phototoxicity, pigmentation and pharmacological effects (NSAID-exacerbated urticaria).

prog: Most simple drug rashes resolve in 1–2 weeks after stopping the drug.
